name: Zane Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Zane, thanks for talking with me. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union or party, and we don't sell anything. What you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me both your public line and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, no problem. I'm a trainee formwork carpenter, so I build the timber and ply moulds that the concrete gets poured into, on a new secondary school going up by the ring road. Day starts at half seven with the toolbox talk, then it's cutting ply, setting up the column boxes, propping, checking levels with the laser, and a lot of waiting for the concrete truck. I like the pour days, when the whole gang's working together and it all has to be right first time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and how does the money side work for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The waiting wears me out, and the shouting when something's a few millimetres out, which with me is still more often than I'd like. I came to this late, I was a delivery driver till twenty-five, so the older lads are miles ahead. Money's thin. I share a house on Carver Road with two mates, I'm still paying off a car loan from my driving days, and I've got about three weeks' bills in the bank on a good month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's sort of how it feels right now, to be fair. Bits and pieces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold. On site I'd say it's a good tool for some things, but it isn't pouring concrete. In the group chat I'd probably post some meme about all the money they spent on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit relieved and a bit disappointed. I use the chat apps now and then, like to check how many ply sheets I need or to sort my CV, and they're handy. But mainly it means I get to learn the trade at the normal speed, which I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the school job and push to get my formwork qualification done by next autumn. I'd try and clear the car loan, which has fourteen months left at about a hundred and sixty a month. I'd keep using the AI apps for small stuff like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the same as now, which isn't amazing, but I know how to live in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be a bit disappointed. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I thought it might make things fairer. Like, the lads who can't read drawings well could get help. If it stays a toy for office people, it just helps the people who already had it easy. That's a bit of a let-down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In this picture, what would make your working life better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady work and a union that actually shows up on our site. Half of us are on agency contracts with no sick pay. That's not an AI problem, that's a politics problem, and it'd still be there.

S0.say: It was oversold, fair enough. It's a good tool for some things, but it isn't pouring concrete, and I'd post a meme about all the money they spent on it.
S0.think: I'd be a bit relieved and a bit disappointed. I use the chat apps now and then and they're handy, but mostly it means I get to learn the trade at the normal speed, which I need.
S0.do: Keeps going on the school job and aims to finish his formwork qualification by next autumn. Tries to clear his car loan, about 160 a month with fourteen months left, and keeps using AI apps for small tasks.
S0.feel: Calm, because life stays the way he already knows how to handle.
S0.quote: If it stays a toy for office people, it just helps the people who already had it easy.
S0.fieldNote: Zane is a late starter in the trade and aware that older colleagues are ahead. Interestingly, he'd be disappointed by a stall because he hoped AI might help less skilled workers. He frames the real problems on site as agency contracts and weak union presence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one I can believe. I've already seen a robot that marks out floor plans on a site in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need training paid for by the companies making the money, and a union deal so it isn't just the agency lads who get dropped. Online I'd share stuff about that, retraining funds and that. I'd try not to be a doom merchant about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job's safer than a lot of jobs, because formwork is messy and every pour's a bit different. But I'm junior and slow, so if a machine speeds up the easy parts, it's the junior easy-parts guy they need less of. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the other firms do for a bit, maybe six months, and see which bits of kit actually stick. Once it's clear, I'd ask to be trained on whatever it is, like the layout robot or the 3D drawing tablet. I'd join the union properly, not just say I'm going to, and I'd carry on paying down the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit of a knot in the stomach, but I'd feel like I had time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait six months. What would you be waiting to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who gets laid off and who gets moved up. If the lads who learn the new kit get kept on, I'm learning it. If they're laying people off anyway, then training doesn't matter and I'd rather spend my energy on the union. I'm not jumping first, I've seen too many gadgets end up in the back of the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, weirdly. She retrained as a teaching assistant at forty when the shoe factory closed. She'd tell me to stop moaning and sign up for the course. She'd be right, too, she normally is.

S1.say: We need training paid for by the companies making the money, and a union deal so it isn't just the agency lads who get dropped. I'd share stuff about retraining funds online without being a doom merchant.
S1.think: Formwork is messy and every pour is different, so it's safer than many jobs. But I'm junior and slow, so if a machine speeds up the easy parts, I'm the easy-parts guy they'll need less of.
S1.do: Watches other firms for about six months to see which equipment sticks, then asks to be trained on it, such as a layout robot or a drawing tablet. Joins the union properly and keeps paying off his car loan.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a knot in his stomach, but he feels there is time.
S1.quote: I'm not jumping first, I've seen too many gadgets end up in the back of the van.
S1.fieldNote: Zane waits for proof, which is his steady streak, but he has a clear trigger for acting: whether learners get kept. His mother's own retraining story is a strong influence. He is honest that his junior status, not his trade, is what makes him exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Wow. That's before I'd even have my ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be stopped or slowed down by law, full stop. I'd say the government needs to pay people a wage while it sorts this out, and that the companies owe that money. I'd be at the march, I'd be sharing petitions, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I'm in real trouble. Three weeks of savings, a car loan, a job I'm not good at yet, and no other building work in town except the school and a retail park. If robots can do formwork and they're cheaper, the gang goes from twelve to two and I'm not one of the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sell the car and clear the loan, even at a loss, and get the bus. I'd sign up for every union meeting and ask the council what support there is. Then I'd look for anything people still want a human for, maybe care work or delivering for the hospital, because two years isn't long enough to finish a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's moving. I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at care work. How would you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, fine. My mum did it for a bit. I'm good with old people, I used to deliver to the same care home every Thursday and have a laugh with them. It's not what I pictured, but I'd rather that than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first, money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, then the phone contract, then the takeaways, in that order. The football subscription would go last, I'm not going to lie. You've got to keep one thing.

S2.say: This has to be stopped or slowed down by law, full stop. The government needs to pay people a wage while it sorts this out, and the companies owe that money.
S2.think: I'd be in real trouble: three weeks of savings, a car loan, a job I'm not good at yet and hardly any other building work in town. If the gang goes from twelve to two, I'm not one of the two.
S2.do: Sells his car in the first month to clear the loan and switches to the bus. Goes to every union meeting, asks the council about support, and looks for work people still want a human for, such as care work or hospital deliveries.
S2.feel: Shaken, as if the floor is moving, and awake at night doing sums.
S2.quote: If robots can do formwork and they're cheaper, the gang goes from twelve to two and I'm not one of the two.
S2.fieldNote: Here Zane moves fast despite usually waiting for proof, because his thin savings force it. He'd switch to care work without much pride getting in the way. His public line is strongly political while the private view is a sober reading of his own position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's still quick, but that's at least long enough to get qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years and we're wasting them if the government doesn't start retraining people now. I'd be pushing the union to get a proper deal on our site. Online I'd probably share more than I talk, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd get my ticket, get a couple of years of decent money, and then have to switch. So the question is what I switch to, and I don't know yet. Nobody really knows what's safe in that picture, I don't think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my formwork qualification and then do a short course in something next to it, maybe running the site machines or doing safety checks, because someone has to sign things off. I'd clear the car in the first year and then try to save a hundred a month. And I'd go to the union meetings properly, monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Pressure, but not panic. I'd feel like I can still steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI apps now and then. Would that change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I'd use them more, once I saw the older lads doing it, to be honest. If Mick the foreman starts using it to check his drawings, I'm doing it the next week. I'd use it to study for the courses, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have in place by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No debt, a few months' money in the bank, and a second skill. That's realistic. Anything more than that, I'd be kidding myself on my wages.

S3.say: We've got five years, and we're wasting them if the government doesn't start retraining people now. I'd be pushing the union to get a proper deal on our site.
S3.think: I'd get my ticket, get a couple of years of decent money, and then have to switch. The question is what I'd switch to, and honestly nobody knows what's safe.
S3.do: Finishes his formwork qualification, then adds a short course in operating site machines or safety checks. Clears the car loan in the first year, saves a hundred a month and attends union meetings monthly.
S3.feel: Anxious and under pressure, but still feeling he can steer.
S3.quote: If Mick the foreman starts using it to check his drawings, I'm doing it the next week.
S3.fieldNote: His steady style shows clearly: he'd adopt AI tools the week after his foreman does, not before. Five years lets him plan in stages: qualification, debt-free, second skill. His goals are modest and he says so frankly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole career change in there, isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same problem but we've got no excuse now, we've got a decade. Public retraining, free courses, a share of the profits. I'd say it like it's normal politics, not an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be all right for a good while. Ten years of formwork, get good, maybe run a small gang, then retrain into something with people while I'm still in my thirties. It's the end bit I can't picture, and I don't think I'm supposed to be able to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, get qualified, and wait a couple of years to see which new jobs actually show up before I pick a course. I'd clear the car, build up maybe six months of savings over five years, and stay in the union. I'd start using the AI tools for planning once the site does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in the back of my head. Mostly I'd get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you'd look at care work. Does that still come up here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe later, around thirty-five. With ten years I'd rather get good at something first, so I've got a story to tell. My mum always says nobody hires a quitter, they hire someone who finished something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you move away for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if all the work's in the city in five years. But my mates are here and my mum's here. I'd only move if I had a job lined up, not on a hope.

S4.say: It's the same problem, but with a decade there's no excuse. Public retraining, free courses and a share of the profits, said like normal politics, not an emergency.
S4.think: I'd be all right for a good while: ten years of formwork, maybe run a small gang, then retrain into something with people while I'm in my thirties. The end bit I can't picture.
S4.do: Keeps going, qualifies, and waits a couple of years to see which new jobs appear before choosing a course. Clears the car and builds roughly six months of savings over five years, stays in the union and starts using AI planning tools once the site does.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background, but mostly getting on with it.
S4.quote: My mum always says nobody hires a quitter, they hire someone who finished something.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Zane wait and build, which fits his steady nature. He'd only move with a job lined up, and his mother's advice shapes much of his thinking. The end point still sits unpictured in the background.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I wouldn't even have finished my ticket and I've got the car loan hanging over me. What would help is a wage from the government while you retrain, a proper one, not a form you fill in for six weeks. And free courses you can do at night, because I can't stop working to learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who's going to be in charge of the robots. If it's the same people who already own everything, it's going to go one way. If the public gets a say, maybe it's different. I'm not sure how, though, I'm just a formwork guy.

headlineQuote: If it's the same people who already own everything, it's going to go one way.
portrait: Zane Rahman is a 27-year-old trainee formwork carpenter on a school build, a former delivery driver who came to the trade late and knows the older crew are ahead of him. He shares a rented house, is paying off a car loan and keeps about three weeks of savings. He is left-leaning and union-minded but waits for proof before changing, and uses AI apps now and then. A stall disappoints him because he hoped AI would help less skilled workers; steady change makes him wait six months and then train up; fast AGI pushes him to sell the car and look at care work; longer warnings let him qualify, clear debt and plan a later switch.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he wouldn't have finished his qualification and his car loan would still be hanging over him.
whatWouldHelp: A proper government wage while retraining, without weeks of forms, and free night courses so he can learn while working.
